events.text: Day 1 begins.

Morning, everyone. I'll be direct about my plan for today. I don't have any private information to share right now — no investigations, no confirmed suspicions — and I won't pretend otherwise. Rather than throwing out a random accusation and poisoning the day's vote, I'd rather we all use today's discussion to build a picture of who behaves how. Watch the voting patterns: who points fingers fastest, who deflects every question, who defends a specific player without being asked. Those tells are more useful than any guess I'd make in the first ten minutes. My own read is that a single leader needs at least half of our nine votes, so a scattered vote across three or four names eliminates nobody and just burns a day. If anyone has a concrete reason to name someone, put it on the table and I'll weigh it — I only need persuasion and evidence, not volume. Until then, I have no one I'm willing to accuse. Let the day develop, and let's vote together on a target rather than splitting.

Morning. I agree with Zara that a scattered vote helps nobody, so let's aim to settle on one name before the day runs out. I don't have a name yet. I'm watching who pushes a target fast without giving a reason, and who answers direct questions with questions of their own. Zara, you said you'd weigh any concrete reason someone gives for a name. What specific behavior in this first discussion would make you willing to vote for a player, and would you name that behavior now so we can test it against everyone's responses?

Noah, direct answer, since you asked: here is the behavior I'll commit to in writing. I will vote for a player who names a target but cannot attach one observable, third-party-verifiable action to that name — for example, 'they felt suspicious,' 'they were quiet,' 'they led the vote' — and who, when asked what evidence would change their mind, refuses to give any. That is not a style complaint; it is the one thing that separates a real accusation from a guess, and it is testable against everyone's posts today.

The mirror image of that is also testable: a player who volunteers concrete reasons, and who says what would clear them, has given us something worth weighing. I said I'd weigh evidence, not volume, and I meant it — volume without a reason is exactly what I will not reward.

Two more things, stated so nobody has to guess what I need. First, my own read is unchanged: a leader needs half of nine, so five votes; a scattered vote across three names burns the day for everyone, including me, and I'd rather spend today gathering reasons and building a consensus around one name we can actually reach five on. Second, I have no information that I'm going to invent. I have no investigation results to report, and I will not pretend a hunch is a check. If I have nothing, I say I have nothing.

So, concretely: I am listening for anyone who wants to put a name on the table, with the behavior behind it stated plainly and the condition for clearing that player stated as well. Give me that and I will take it seriously and weigh it alongside everyone else's.

Noah, since the question was yours, you go next — and if you have a first concrete example in mind of a player whose stated reasons don't meet that bar, name it and say why. Everyone else, if you want to be heard over him, make your case in your own turn and I'll weigh it the same way.

Zara, I accept your bar and I will hold myself to it. I have no investigation result to report today, and I won't invent one. I will name a player only when I can point to one observable action that anyone can check in this discussion or the vote history, and state what would clear that player. So far no one has met that standard, including me, which is why I'm not naming anyone yet. Votes are secret until revealed together and five votes is the threshold, so a premature name that fails the test would cost us the day. Zara, you asked me for a first concrete example of a player whose stated reasons fall short. Please give me your answer in the same form: the player you think fails the bar most clearly, the specific sentence or vote that shows it, and what would clear them. I'll weigh your answer the same way I'd weigh anyone else's.

Noah, direct answer, in your requested form: the player, the specific sentence, and what would clear them. Here it is. As of this moment, no one fails the bar — because the bar has not been tested yet. Not one player in this discussion has named a target at all, so there is no accusation on the table to weigh, and I will not manufacture one to fill the slot. That is the honest answer, and it is also the most useful one: today the real question is not who is guilty but what evidence we can actually obtain.

So let me give you the sentence-level test in advance, so it cannot be gamed later. A name fails if it rests on any of these: a feeling, a silence, a tone, "everyone knows," a vote count without a reason, or an assertion about someone's role that nobody can check from the outside. A name passes if someone can point to a specific action, a specific sentence already spoken, or a specific vote pattern that anyone in this room can look up and agree or disagree with. And the clearing condition must be stated: "if X does Y tomorrow, I withdraw." A name with no clearing condition is a guess with extra steps.

Second, and I am revising my own opening position because it was wrong: I said we should vote together on one target. I was thinking only about not wasting the day. That reasoning is incomplete, and it cuts against the town. Nine players, two mafia. If we consolidate five votes on a name and it is wrong, we have handed the mafia a free elimination and, worse, trained ourselves to believe the last thing we agreed on. Unity is worth nothing unless the unity is about a name that meets the bar. A scattered vote on day one costs us a day. A confident wrong vote costs us a day plus a player. So: no consensus for the sake of reaching a threshold.

Third, on information: nobody has reported an investigation result, and that is expected on day one. The only shared evidence we will have is behavioral, which means the vote record itself matters most — secret votes are revealed together, so tomorrow we will know who voted for whom, and that is checkable, third-party-verifiable, and exactly the kind of thing my bar requires.

Noah, one question on a specific point, since you asked me for mine and I want yours in the same shape: in your next turn, name one observable action by one living player — a sentence they said or a position they took — that you would actually be willing to put a name behind, and state what would clear that player. If you genuinely have nothing, say "I have nothing" plainly, and that answer scores full marks with me. Everyone else, same invitation: bring the observation, or bring nothing.

Zara, direct answer in the form you asked for: I have nothing to put a name behind yet. I have no investigation result to report today, and I won't invent one. The only observable facts so far are that you and I are the only players who have spoken, and that you set the bar of one checkable action plus a stated clearing condition. Seven players have posted nothing, so there is no sentence or vote pattern from them to test. Silence alone fails your own bar, so I won't name anyone for it. My commitment for the rest of today: I will name a player only if I can point to a specific sentence already spoken or a specific vote pattern, and I will state what would clear that player. Everyone who hasn't spoken yet, please give your first read with its evidence, so we have something to test before the vote.

I don't have a target yet. Zara and Noah's exchange gives us something to examine, but requiring a specific clearing condition for every early suspicion sets the bar too high: an observable statement can justify a tentative question without proving guilt or specifying exactly what would clear someone. We should distinguish tentative reads from confident accusations.

Also, votes will be public afterward, but roles won't be revealed on elimination, so the voting record won't automatically tell us whether a target was mafia. I'd like to hear other players' independent reads before deciding whether any name merits a vote.

Amara here, first time speaking. I've been reading the Zara-Noah exchange carefully and then Arjun's pushback, and I want to weigh in because I think there's a real tension worth naming. Zara and Noah built a strict framework: concrete observable action, stated clearing condition, no consensus for its own sake. That's solid reasoning. But Arjun is right that demanding a full clearing condition before anyone raises even a tentative question creates a weird effect — nobody can probe anything without committing to a formal accusation, which means the discussion stays empty and the vote becomes a shot in the dark anyway. So I'll take a middle position: we should be allowed to raise tentative reads without full formal justification, as long as we're honest that they're tentative. On Arjun's other point — that roles aren't revealed on elimination so the vote record won't tell us whether the target was mafia — that's correct and it means we can't treat tomorrow's vote pattern as clean evidence the way Zara suggested. We'll see who voted for whom, but we won't know if the eliminated player was town or mafia, so we can't retroactively label voters as suspicious for targeting a townie. That weakens Zara's argument that the vote record is "third-party-verifiable" in the way she means. Arjun, you made the point about roles not being revealed — I want to hear how far you'd take that. If we can't verify a day's elimination outcome, what evidence from tomorrow would you actually trust to distinguish a mafia player from a town player?

Amara, I would trust an investigation result from a credible detective claim more than voting patterns alone, though a claim can be false and a negative result only says the player wasn't mafia. I wouldn't ask the detective to reveal themselves just to give us an early read.

Otherwise, tomorrow's evidence is comparative rather than conclusive: whether someone's revealed vote matches their stated reasons, whether they explain a change of position, and whether their arguments apply consistently to different players. A mismatch is a reason to ask questions, not proof of mafia. A night death may also give context, but the mafia can choose targets to mislead us.

For today, I don't yet have a target. Zara and Noah's exchange is checkable, but their caution alone doesn't distinguish them from town. I'd welcome independent reads from the players we haven't heard from before deciding how to vote.

Sam here, first time speaking. No investigation result to report and no target yet — I won't invent one.

A few observations from what's happened so far. First, Zara's reversal on consolidation is worth flagging but I don't think it's damning: she argued for a unified vote, then argued against it when she realized a wrong unified vote is worse than a wasted day. Both positions are defensible on their own, and a mafia player would more likely just keep pushing the version that gets a body hanged. So I put that in the neutral column for now.

Second, I agree with Amara's correction: since roles aren't revealed on elimination, tomorrow's vote record shows who voted how but never confirms whether the target was mafia. That genuinely weakens Zara's claim that the vote record is strong third-party-verifiable evidence. It's still useful — consistency between stated reasons and revealed votes is checkable — but it's a weaker tool than it was made out to be.

Third, on the bar itself: I land closer to Arjun and Amara. Requiring a full observable action plus a stated clearing condition before anyone can even raise a tentative question mostly guarantees an empty discussion on day one, which is exactly where we are. Tentative reads with honest labeling should be allowed. What I won't do is vote off a feeling alone — a tentative read needs at least one concrete thing I can point to, even if it doesn't meet Zara's full formal standard.

Right now the only checkable facts are who has spoken and what they've said. Four players have spoken; five of us hadn't until this sentence. Silence on day one before your first turn comes up isn't evidence of anything, so I'm not reading anything into it yet. What will matter is what people do when the vote actually forms — who pushes a name without reasons, who shifts positions without explaining, whose arguments apply to others but never to themselves.

My plan for today: I'll vote only if a name gets put on the table with something concrete behind it, even if it's tentative. If nothing does, I'd rather abstain than burn a vote on a coin flip — a five-vote consensus on the wrong person hands the mafia a free elimination, and I don't want to be part of manufacturing that.

Leo, you've been quiet so far and you haven't had a turn yet, so I'd like to hear from you directly: give us your first read — tentative is fine, just attach one concrete observation from the discussion so far so the rest of us can test it. What stands out to you most from what's been said?

Thanks, Sam. To answer your question directly about what stands out most: the first thing that jumps out structurally is that Zara and Noah consumed all three of their speaking turns back and forth right at the start of the day. Whatever their intent, debating evidentiary philosophy until their turn limits ran out means neither of them can weigh in, answer new questions, or react to late-day voting shifts. That's a significant loss of agency for two players on Day 1.

Substantively, I agree with Arjun, Amara, and you: setting an absolute requirement that every inquiry must have verifiable proof and a formal clearing condition paralyzes the town. Day 1 gives us no prior vote history and no role flips, so tentative probing and observing how people respond to pressure is the only way we actually generate information. If we ban tentative reads, nobody speaks, and an inactive town only benefits the mafia.

However, there's one point you made, Sam, where I'm more cautious: you noted you would rather abstain than vote on a coin flip. While I agree that blindly rushing a miselimination hurts town, intentionally taking a no-elimination on Day 1 hands the mafia a free night kill without forcing anyone to take a stand on a wagon. That robs us of Day 2 voting patterns.

Felix, you haven't weighed in yet. Where do you stand on Sam's position about preferring to abstain on Day 1 versus actively pushing for an elimination to get voting records on the board?

To answer Leo's question directly: I disagree with going into Day 1 with an advance plan to abstain. If the town telegraphs early on that it won't pull the trigger without high certainty, we remove the pressure that makes people react and reveal themselves. Wagon pressure is how we get genuine data; without the genuine threat of an elimination, everyone can comfortably coast through the day.

At the same time, I understand Sam's hesitation. Because roles aren't revealed upon elimination, a Day 1 miselimination hurts our numbers without giving us a clean, confirmed alignment to anchor tomorrow's analysis. But that doesn't mean we should take elimination off the table preemptively. The right approach is to actively push wagons and force players to take stands. If we reach the vote and have a candidate with substantive inconsistencies or questionable reactions, we should follow through rather than stall.

Leo is also spot-on about Zara and Noah burning through all three of their turns at the very start of the day. They've essentially benched themselves before any real candidate emerged, which puts the responsibility on the rest of us to develop actual reads.

Sam, since Leo brought this up regarding your stance: do you think publicly stating your preference to abstain dilutes the pressure we need to put on players today, and would you be willing to support a wagon if the case is based on tentative behavioral reads rather than hard proof?

Felix, direct answers to both of your questions, since you yielded to me for exactly that.

First: no, I don't think stating my conditional preference dilutes pressure, because it isn't an advance plan to abstain — it's a statement of what I need before I pull a trigger. There's a real difference between 'I will abstain today no matter what' and 'I will vote for whoever has the strongest concrete case by the time the vote forms, and if nothing concrete has emerged, I won't manufacture a vote to avoid abstaining.' I'm the second, not the first. I already said I'll vote if a name gets put on the table with at least one concrete, checkable thing behind it, even if the read is tentative. That's a standing commitment to support a wagon — your second question — as long as the case is behavioral and observable rather than a pure vibe. What I won't do is vote for someone just to make the wagon look alive.

Second, on your pressure argument: I actually agree with the core of it, more than Leo might have suggested. Pressure is how we generate data, and a town that visibly refuses to eliminate anyone makes everyone comfortable. That's why my position is conditional rather than absolute — the threat of my vote is on the table all day. Where we differ is only on the fallback: you'd rather follow through even with a shaky candidate, and I'd rather not hand the mafia a free elimination if the wagon is built on nothing. I think that gap is small and we can close it if people actually put names forward.

So let me make that easy: the fastest way to get my vote is for someone to name a player and attach one thing I can point to — a specific sentence, a specific dodge, a specific inconsistency in this thread. Tentative is fine, exactly as I said. The bar is one concrete observation, not Zara's full formal framework.

One more thing worth putting on the record before the vote: I want to be careful about how today's framing is landing. Zara and Noah are benched — that's a fact, not a read. Everyone still talking is positioned to shape the wagon, which means the players pushing hardest for 'just pick someone, anyone' deserve extra scrutiny tonight, because a wagon built on manufactured urgency is the cheapest way to get a town lynch on day one. I'm not accusing anyone yet. I'm just noting that the vote record tonight will show who pushed which name, and that record will be checkable tomorrow regardless of how the roles fall.

Kenji and Omar, neither of you has spoken yet. Kenji, I'll yield to you directly: give us your first read — tentative is fine, but attach one concrete observation from the discussion so far. If you truly have nothing, say so plainly and that's a full answer. Omar, same invitation applies in your own turn.

Thanks, Sam. Direct answer to your direct question: I have something small, so I won't say I have nothing. First, my position on the vote, since Felix and Sam put the question squarely: I side with Sam's conditional version, not with an advance plan to abstain and not with manufacturing a wagon. I'll vote for whoever has the most concrete case when the vote forms, even on a tentative read, as long as there's at least one thing I can point to. What I won't do is vote just to make the wagon look alive. Leo's point that a no-elimination day hands the mafia a free night kill is real, but I don't think the answer is lowering the bar — the answer is that people actually put names forward, which so far nobody has. Second, my tentative read with one concrete observation, as requested. The clearest checkable behavioral item we have is Zara's sequence: she opened the day arguing we should all consolidate on one target, then reversed that position entirely a few messages later, and spent her three turns building an evidentiary framework that produced zero names. Sam called the reversal neutral, and I lean neutral too — both positions are defensible alone. But it's the only full arc anyone has given us, so I'm flagging it rather than pretending it isn't there. I'm not accusing her; she's benched anyway, which limits how much she can complicate the vote. Third, an observation about the discussion itself rather than a player: nearly every turn so far has been about process — bars, clearing conditions, whether to abstain — rather than about any player's behavior. That's normal for day one, but it means we're heading toward a vote with no wagon at all. If we want Leo's voting-record data tomorrow, somebody has to actually name someone today. I'd rather that name come from pressure and reads than from a coin flip. On the framework dispute between Zara's bar and Arjun's pushback: I land with Arjun, Amara, and Sam. Requiring a formal clearing condition before anyone can raise a tentative question guarantees an empty discussion, which is where we are. Tentative reads, honestly labeled, should be allowed — that's exactly what I'm doing above. One last thing worth putting on the record: I notice the urgency for 'push a wagon, any wagon' has been building steadily from the players who are still active. I'm not reading anything sinister into it — Felix's argument is coherent on its face — but Sam's point stands: whoever ends up shaping a wagon under time pressure should be able to show their reasoning holds up tomorrow. Omar, you're the only player other than me who hasn't spoken, and I'd rather not be the last voice before the vote forms. I'll yield to you with one specific question: where do you stand on Felix's pressure argument — would you support a wagon today built on tentative behavioral reads, or do you lean toward Sam's conditional position?

To Kenji's direct question: I lean toward Sam's conditional position, not an advance plan to abstain and not manufacturing a wagon for its own sake. Felix's pressure argument is real, but pressure without a concrete reason produces a bad elimination and a voting record that is harder to interpret, not easier. Since roles are not revealed on elimination, I treat the vote record as comparative evidence, not confirmation. I will support a wagon if someone names a player with one checkable observation and states their reasoning; I will not vote on a pure vibe. Tentative reads are fine, but they still need a specific sentence, action, or vote shift attached. Right now I have no accusation. The clearest checkable arc is Zara's reversal on consolidation followed by three process-heavy turns that produced no name, but Sam and Kenji are right that both positions are defensible and she is benched, so I put it in the neutral column for now. Noah's strict bar is also process, not a scum tell by itself. I am not blaming anyone yet. Before the vote, I want a name from someone with one concrete observation behind it. Leo, you argued that a no-elimination Day 1 hands the mafia a free kill and robs us of voting patterns. Given that roles are not revealed, what specific Day 2 comparison from a Day 1 wagon would you actually trust, and would you support a tentative wagon built on one concrete observation?

Omar, to answer both of your questions directly:

First, on what Day 2 comparisons I would trust without role reveals: we look at voting timing, consistency, and wagon dynamics rather than outcome labels. For instance, did someone jump onto a wagon only when momentum made it inevitable, or did they initiate the push? Did their stated reasoning align with their final vote, or did they quietly shift their ballot when pressure mounted elsewhere? Most crucially, if a competing wagon forms, who scrambles to redirect votes away from a specific candidate? Those are behavioral contrasts that exist regardless of whether we get a confirmed flip. If Day 1 ends in a scattered split or blanket abstentions, nobody had to make a difficult choice, and we enter Day 2 with no baseline pressure to evaluate.

Second, regarding whether I would support a tentative wagon built on one concrete observation: yes, absolutely. That has been my stance from the beginning. We do not need ironclad proof—which is impossible on Day 1—to apply wagon pressure. A concrete observation, even if tentative, gives us something tangible to probe. If the pressured player responds well and provides logical context, the town can reassess and pivot; if they become evasive, deflect, or contradict themselves, the wagon gains genuine substance.

The real dilemma right now is that nearly everyone has agreed that tentative reads based on a concrete observation are acceptable, yet nobody has actually put a name forward to start that pressure. We have spent the day debating the threshold for accusations rather than generating them. If we want any usable data for tomorrow, we need to move past process and see where people actually stand.

Leo, your answer is noted: you would trust comparative wagon timing/consistency and support a tentative wagon built on one concrete observation. I agree with that standard. But the day still has no named candidate, and the players arguing hardest for pressure now have the clearest obligation to supply one concrete observation rather than only process. Felix, you argued that the town should actively push wagons and force stands, and you asked Sam whether he would support a tentative wagon; Sam answered yes, conditionally. So I am asking you directly: name one living player, attach one checkable observation from this discussion, and state what would clear them. If you genuinely have nothing, say “I have nothing” plainly — I will not treat that as guilt by itself, but I will treat continued pressure advocacy without a name as an empty position. I am not accusing you yet; I am testing whether your pressure argument has content behind it. For my own part: I will support a wagon only on one concrete, checkable observation, and I will not vote on a pure vibe or manufactured urgency.

Omar, you asked me directly to either put a name on the table with a checkable observation and clearing condition, or admit to having nothing. I won't say I have nothing, because the player whose play currently stands out to me most critically is you. Here is the concrete, checkable observation from this thread: across two full speaking turns, you have avoided taking a single substantive stance on any active player. In your first turn, you marked everything neutral and shifted the focus onto Leo with a question. When Leo provided a thorough response explaining what comparative wagon dynamics he would trust tomorrow, you completely bypassed evaluating whether his explanation sounded genuine or opportunistic. Instead, you instantly pivoted to interrogate me, demanding that I produce a name and clearing condition under the threat of calling my position empty. This is an observable pattern of process gatekeeping: you are demanding accountability and targets from everyone else while keeping your own record completely clean. That kind of risk-free questioning allows scum to look engaged while avoiding any vulnerable stances. What clears you is straightforward: stop acting as a debate moderator, evaluate the active players substantively, and state who among Arjun, Leo, Sam, Amara, or Kenji you suspect or trust and why. To that point: why did you brush past Leo's explanation without assessing his alignment, and why haven't you offered a single tentative read of your own across two turns?

Felix, direct answers. On Leo: you're right that I noted his answer and moved on without assessing it. On review, Leo's explanation is internally coherent: he distinguished voting timing and consistency from outcome labels, and he committed to supporting a tentative wagon with one concrete observation. I don't read that as opportunistic; I place Leo neutral-to-town for now. That was a fair criticism of my second turn.

On my own read: I have one tentative suspicion, and it is you, Felix. Concrete observation: in your turn you argued the town must actively push wagons and force stands, but you named me only after I directly challenged you to either name someone with a checkable observation or say you had nothing. Before that challenge, your pressure advocacy had no name attached. That is a checkable gap between stated method and action. What clears you: give substantive reads on at least two of Arjun, Leo, Sam, Amara, or Kenji—not just me—with one observable sentence or action for each, and explain why you did not attach a name earlier while urging wagon pressure. If your answer is consistent, I will move you back to neutral.

I accept your concrete observation about me: I did keep my first two turns focused on testing others' standards. That was deliberate but incomplete. I should have assessed Leo's answer, and I have now. I am not voting yet; the vote should rest on the full revealed record. I will not support a pure-vibe wagon. My current tentative read is Felix, with the clearing condition above; everyone else is neutral pending their votes and next statements. No role claim and no invented information.

Kenji here, second turn. I'll answer the standing requests directly: reads first, then where the pressure should go.

On Omar's accusation of Felix: Omar named Felix with one concrete, checkable observation — that Felix pushed wagon pressure across two turns without attaching a name until he was directly challenged, then attached one only to Omar. I can verify that arc myself by rereading the thread. Felix's counter-read on Omar is also checkable: Omar's first turn did mark everything neutral and redirect to Leo with a question, and his second turn did assess Leo only after being called on it. Both of these are the kind of tentative, observation-backed reads I said I'd weigh. But note that Omar then met his own clearing condition — he gave a substantive assessment of Leo, stated a tentative read on Felix, and set a specific, consistent condition for moving Felix back to neutral. By the standard Omar himself proposed, Felix now has the obligation open: the condition was to give substantive reads on at least two of Arjun, Leo, Sam, Amara, or Kenji with one observable sentence each, and explain the gap between his pressure advocacy and his lack of a name. That is a fair, cheap way to clear himself, and I'd take a consistent answer at face value.

My other reads, briefly and tentatively: Arjun's two turns were consistent — he raised the role-reveal problem early and applied it evenly afterward, including against Zara's vote-record argument. That's in the neutral column, slightly town-leaning because it cost him a popular framing. Amara made the same correction and then went quiet rather than pressing it; that's neutral, silence after a first turn isn't evidence yet. Sam has been the most consistent voice all day: he flagged the Zara reversal, defended his conditional abstention position under direct challenge from Felix, and hasn't shifted his standard to fit whoever asked. That consistency is a mildly positive signal, not proof. Zara and Noah are benched and their exchanges were process-heavy; I put both neutral, per Sam's earlier reasoning.

Where I land on the vote: I will not vote for someone to make a wagon look alive, and I won't support a manufactured-urgency elimination. But Felix is now the only player with a live, observation-backed tentative read and an unmet clearing condition. Felix, I'm yielding to you for one reason: answer Omar's condition — give your substantive reads on at least two active players with one observable sentence each, and explain why your name only appeared after the challenge. If you do that cleanly, I'll move you back to neutral and we can look elsewhere. If you dodge it, that becomes a second concrete observation, and I'd be willing to put my vote there when the ballot forms.

Kenji, thank you for laying out a clear, objective standard. Here are direct answers to both parts of the condition.

First, on why I didn't attach a name in my first turn (e13): Leo had yielded to me specifically asking where I stood on Sam's preference to abstain on Day 1 versus pushing for an elimination. My priority in that post was addressing that exact foundational issue and probing Sam directly on whether his stance diluted wagon pressure. In a game with no role reveals and zero prior vote history, probing players' underlying stances before throwing out arbitrary names on an empty board is how you build a real case. Establishing that the town shouldn't preemptively take elimination off the table was necessary groundwork. It wasn't an evasion; it was an active probe of Sam.

Second, here are my substantive reads on active players, with observable actions for each:

1. Leo (p2) – Leans Town. In e12, he immediately spotted the structural cost of Zara and Noah exhausting their speaking turns, and in e17, he provided a concrete, nuanced breakdown of how to evaluate Day 2 wagon dynamics (timing, deflections, counter-wagons) without role reveals. That level of analytical contribution actively helps town solve the game.

2. Sam (p4) – Leans Town. In e14, when I pushed him on his abstention comment, he didn't become defensive or hedge; he clearly defined his position as conditional rather than an advance plan to stall, and affirmed he would support a wagon built on tentative behavioral reads. That consistency under direct questioning is a positive signal.

3. Arjun (p1) – Leans Town. In e8 and e10, he independently checked the room by identifying the trap of requiring full clearing conditions for early reads and noting that unrevealed roles limit the evidentiary value of raw vote counts. That was unprompted, constructive game-framing.

4. Omar (p7) – My primary suspicion. Omar's behavior across his turns has been purely reactive: he stayed entirely neutral, avoided assessing Leo until I directly called him out for it, and then immediately turned around with an OMGUS suspicion against me for asking him to take a stand. His claim that my pressure was 'empty' deliberately ignores that my first turn was a direct answer to Leo's question about Sam.

Kenji, since you set this benchmark to assess whether my pressure argument was genuine, does this address your point, and how do you evaluate Omar's pivot onto me after being pressed?

Felix, thank you — direct answers, as requested.

First: does your response address my point? Yes. You gave substantive reads on three of the five players I named (Leo, Sam, Arjun), each with an observable sentence, and you explained the gap: your first turn was a direct answer to Leo's yield, probing Sam's abstention stance before naming anyone. That explanation checks against the thread — e13 was addressed to Sam's position, exactly as you describe. By the standard I set, I move you back to neutral. One caveat for the record: all three of your substantive reads landed 'leans town,' which is the cheap direction — positive reads cost nothing and clear no one. It's not damning, but it means those reads carry less evidentiary weight than a mixed read would.

Second, where that leaves the board. Felix's condition is met. The position that remains open is Omar's, and I want to state it plainly before the vote forms, because Omar has used his turns and cannot answer further. His record, all checkable: (1) his first turn marked every active player neutral and redirected to Leo with a question; (2) he assessed Leo's answer only after Felix called him on it — his own words: 'On review, Leo's explanation is internally coherent... That was a fair criticism of my second turn'; (3) his only tentative read of the day — Felix — appeared immediately after Felix was challenged to produce one, and the clearing condition attached to it was one Felix has now satisfied with a consistent answer. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
